title: The Sleeping Hymn
premise: Marguerite Amberdale hosts a small-town overnight radio show, and for twelve years the calls have come from listeners who died days earlier — voices he has explained away as grief, hoaxes, and bad phone lines. When an excavation crew beneath the old Amberdale chapel unearths a door sealed from the inside, the dead callers begin naming him: the last of the family that took something in 1974 and buried it alive. Pulled into the excavation by a frost that writes hymn-notes across every window, Marguerite must descend past the door with his found family — his producer Devi, a retired gravedigger named Ossie, and a teenage caller who should be dead but isn't — to return what was taken. The ending demands he give back not just the stolen relic but the twelve years of borrowed life it bought him; he survives only because the found family refuses to let him pay alone, splitting the debt between them as the frost finishes its final pattern.
about_author: Xanthe Galloway is the pen name of a former late-night radio engineer who spent a decade in stations that hummed at frequencies no dial explained. They write horror about inheritance, small towns, and the things families agree not to hear.

chapters.title: Dead Air, Warm Voices
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A routine broadcast is interrupted by a call from Ellen Marsh, who drowned six days ago; she asks him to stop pretending. He logs it as a prank, but his hands shake through sign-off. Emotional beat: the crack in twelve years of rationalization finally shows.

chapters.title: The Excavation Below the Chapel
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. The production team visits the Amberdale chapel dig site for a live segment; workers have hit a stone door with hinges on the inside. Marguerite's surname makes the foreman stare. Emotional beat: unease curdling into recognition that this story is about him.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, flashback-woven. He recounts the first dead caller in 2013 and the system he built to survive them: tapes, alibis, denial. Devi finds his archive and realizes he's known all along. Emotional beat: shame exposed; the cost of survival made visible.

chapters.title: Frost in July
chapters.summary: Ossie's POV. The retired gravedigger finds hymn-notes etched in frost on the chapel windows in midsummer, matching a pattern from 1974 he helped bury. He brings photographs to the station. Emotional beat: dread arriving through an old man's quiet certainty.

chapters.title: The Caller Who Should Be Dead
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Teenager Wren calls in mid-broadcast, describing her own funeral happening tomorrow; she sounds alive, terrified, and knows the station's dead-caller secret. She asks to meet. Emotional beat: fear giving way to a first flicker of responsibility.

chapters.title: What Grandfather Took
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. Researching the 1974 closure of the chapel, she finds a suppressed report: nine choir members sealed inside during a 'renovation,' and an Amberdale ledger listing a removed reliquary. Emotional beat: the family sin takes shape — theft dressed as rescue.

chapters.title: Wren at the Door
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Meeting Wren, he confirms she is warm, breathing, impossible — the frost pattern on her skin matches the chapel windows. The dead callers' voices now bleed through her phone when it's off. Emotional beat: denial collapses; he chooses to help.

chapters.title: The Choir Rehearses
chapters.summary: Ossie's POV. At night the excavation crew hears nine-part harmony under the earth; two workers walk into the pit and are found at dawn, frost-patterned, smiling. Ossie recognizes the hymn: the one the 1974 choir sang as the door closed. Emotional beat: the past stops being history.

chapters.title: Sign-Off Interrupted
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Mid-broadcast, all nine dead callers speak at once, harmonizing, addressing him by his childhood name. The station lights die; frost climbs the mixing desk. Devi pulls him out as the transmitter plays the hymn alone. Emotional beat: hunted.

chapters.title: The Ledger's Last Page
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. In the Amberdale house she finds the final ledger entry: the reliquary was never returned because returning it meant dying — grandfather traded the choir's lives for his own line's longevity. Twelve years of Marguerite's health were bought twice over. Emotional beat: fury at inheritance.

chapters.title: Ossie's Confession
chapters.summary: Ossie's POV. He admits he was the apprentice who mortared the door shut in 1974, told the choir was already dead. He wasn't sure. He has heard them ever since. Emotional beat: guilt shared halved; the found family forms around confession.

chapters.title: Wren's Funeral
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. They attend Wren's funeral; her body lies in the casket while she stands beside it, visible only to those marked by frost. The congregation sings the hymn without knowing why. Emotional beat: grief and wonder braided; stakes turn personal.

chapters.title: The Pattern Completes
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. Mapping frost occurrences town-wide, she realizes they trace the hymn's score toward completion — each death adds a note. When the last note lands, the door opens from either side. Emotional beat: a deadline becomes real and arithmetic.

chapters.title: What the Reliquary Holds
chapters.summary: Ossie's POV. Recovered from the 1974 evidence locker, the reliquary is opened: inside, not bones but breath — nine preserved exhalations, the choir's last songs kept warm so the Amberdales could keep living off them. Emotional beat: horror refined into pity.

chapters.title: The Bargain Refused
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The dead callers offer terms: return the reliquary alone and Marguerite dies in the choir's place, clean and final. He almost accepts. Devi and Ossie refuse to let him. Emotional beat: the price of survival named aloud and contested.

chapters.title: Descent Preparations
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. The four prepare: salt lines, tape recorders running hot, Wren's frost-marked skin as compass. Ossie teaches them the hymn — not to sing along, but to know when it changes. Emotional beat: frightened people choosing each other anyway.

chapters.title: Through the Door Sealed From Inside
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The descent: the door opens inward at their approach, revealing a chapel interior untouched since 1974, candles still soft, nine chairs facing an empty altar. The frost follows them down like weather. Emotional beat: awe weaponized into terror.

chapters.title: The Nine
chapters.summary: Wren's POV (her first). She sees the choir clearly where the others see shadows; they are not angry, only unfinished, mid-hymn for fifty years. They ask Wren — half-dead, half-alive — to finish the verse. Emotional beat: compassion inside the horror.

chapters.title: The Verse Unfinished
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. To finish the hymn requires a voice given freely, which means surrendering the borrowed years. Marguerite begins to sing; his body starts failing note by note, aging the twelve years back. Emotional beat: sacrifice embraced without drama.

chapters.title: Splitting the Debt
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. As Marguerite's voice frays, Devi, Ossie, and Wren join the verse uninvited, dividing the payment four ways — the debt of survival shared until none of it kills. The choir exhales its nine breaths back into the reliquary. Emotional beat: found family as literal salvation.

chapters.title: The Final Pattern
chapters.summary: Ossie's POV. The frost completes its score across the chapel ceiling and stops; the door swings wide onto morning. The choir, finished, goes quiet — not gone, but released. Ossie lays his mortar trowel on the altar and leaves it there. Emotional beat: release after fifty years of complicity.

chapters.title: Sign-On
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, epilogue. Weeks later, the show returns — renamed, four voices at the desk instead of one. The dead no longer call; instead, listeners who are simply lonely do, and Marguerite answers honestly. On the last frost of autumn, one window holds a single note: thanks. Emotional beat: survival redefined as something shared.
